[[File:Circle_radians_tau.gif|thumb|An arc of a circle with the same length as the radius of that circle corresponds to an angle of 1&nbsp;radian. A full circle corresponds to a full turn, or approximately 6.28&nbsp;radians, which is expressed here using the Greek letter [[tau]] ({{math|''τ''}}).]]
[[File:Degree-Radian Conversion tau.svg|right|thumb|A comparison of angles expressed in degrees and radians]]

The number {{math|'''''τ'''''}} ({{IPAc-en|'|t|aʊ|,_|'|t|ɔː|,_|'|t|ɒ|audio=LL-Q1860 (eng)-Flame, not lame-Tau.wav}}; spelled out as '''tau''') is a [[mathematical constant]], equal to 2[[pi|{{math|''π''}}]], that has been proposed as an alternative to [[pi|{{math|''π''}}]] by various proponents, who argue that [[mathematical notation]] would be simpler, clearer or pedagogically preferable if formulas and quantities (including [[angle]]s) were described in terms of {{math|''τ''}} instead of {{math|''π''}}. A constant named tau is implemented in some [[programming language]]s and calculator apps as an alias for 2{{math|''π''}}. {{math|''τ''}} is approximately equal to

{{block indent|{{gaps|6.28318|53071|79586|47692|52867|66559|00576|83943|38798|75021|16419...}}}}

It is the [[ratio]] of a [[circle]]'s [[circumference]] to its [[radius]], whereas {{math|''π''}} instead corresponds to the ratio of a circle's circumference to its [[diameter]]. Like {{math|''π''}}, {{math|''τ''}} can be defined in several other equivalent ways: notably, {{math|''τ''}} is equal to the [[periodic function|period]] of the complex [[exponential function]]. Like {{math|''π''}}, {{math|''τ''}} is [[irrational number|irrational]] and [[transcendental number|transcendental]].

While {{math|''π''}} is used almost exclusively in mainstream mathematical education and practice, it has been proposed in recent decades, most notably by physicist [[Michael Hartl]] in his 2010 article ''The Tau Manifesto'', that {{math|''τ''}} should be used instead. Hartl and other proponents argue that {{math|''τ''}} is the more natural circle constant and its use leads to conceptually simpler and more intuitive mathematical notation; in particular, {{math|''τ''}} is the angle measure of a whole [[turn (angle)|turn]] in [[radian]]s, whereas {{math|''π''}} corresponds only to a half-turn, so proponents argue that angles in radians are more intuitive when expressed as fractions of {{math|''τ''}} compared to {{math|''π''}}.<ref name="Hartl_2019" />

Critics have responded that the benefits of using {{math|''τ''}} over {{math|''π''}} are trivial and that given the ubiquity and historical significance of {{math|''π''}} a change is unlikely to occur.<ref name="Telegraph_2011" />

The proposal did not initially gain widespread acceptance in the mathematical community, but awareness of {{math|''τ''}} has become more widespread,<ref name="McMillan_2020" /> including having been added to several major programming languages and calculators.

== Fundamentals ==

=== Geometric definitions ===
The number {{math|''τ''}} can be defined as the [[ratio]] of the [[circumference]] to the [[radius]] of a [[circle]]:<math display="block"> \tau = \frac{\mbox{circumference}}{\mbox{radius}}.</math> (The ratio {{math|{{sfrac|circumference|radius}}}} is constant regardless of the circle's size, designating {{math|''τ''}} as the fixed ratio between the circumference and the radius of any circle.)

The ratio of a circle's circumference to its radius can be related to the number [[pi|{{math|''π''}}]]: <math display="block">\pi = \frac{\mbox{circumference}}{\mbox{diameter}} = \frac{\mbox{circumference}}{2 \cdot \mbox{radius}} = \frac{\tau}{2},</math> showing that {{math|''τ''}} equals {{math|2''π''}}. Accordingly, the number {{math|''τ''}} shares many of the properties of {{math|''π''}}, including being a [[transcendental number]] and hence also [[irrational number|irrational]].

[[File:Tau-angles.svg|thumb|right|Some special angles in radians, stated in terms of {{math|''τ''}}]]
When [[radian]]s are used as the unit of [[angle|angular measure]], there are {{math|''τ''}} radians in one full [[turn (angle)|turn]] of a circle, and fractions of {{math|''τ''}} correspond (in radians) to angles that are the same fractions of a turn: for instance, {{math|{{sfrac|1|8}}''τ'' rad}} is an eighth of a turn; {{math|{{sfrac|3|4}}''τ'' rad}} is three-quarters of a turn.

=== Other definitions ===
Like {{math|''π''}}, {{math|''τ''}} can also be defined analytically, in terms of integrals, series or trigonometric functions.

{{math|''τ''}} can be defined as the smallest positive real number {{math|''x''}} such that {{math|1=[[Sine and cosine|cos]](''x'') = 1}}, or as the [[periodic function|period]] of the [[sine and cosine]] functions. Equivalently, {{math|''τ''}} can be defined as the period of the complex [[exponential function]], which shares the same period as the sine and cosine functions as shown by [[Euler's formula]]. (The sine, cosine and exponential functions themselves can be defined independently of geometry using [[Taylor series]], allowing to define {{math|''τ''}} without any reference to circles or geometry.)

Other formulas equal to {{math|''τ''}} include [[integral]]s such as {{tmath|\textstyle \int_{-2}^{2} \sqrt{4 - x^2} \, dx }} (which is half the area of a circle of radius 2), or sums of [[infinite series]], such as the [[Gregory series]]: <math display="block">\tau = 8 \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n}}{2n+1} = 8 - \frac{8}{3} + \frac{8}{5} - \frac{8}{7} + \frac{8}{9}...</math> More series definitions can be found at ''[[List of formulae involving π|List of formulae involving {{math|π}}]]''.

===Digits of {{math|''τ''}}===
The first 51 decimal digits of {{math|''τ''}} are: {{gaps|6.28318|53071|79586|47692|52867|66559|00576|83943|38798|75021...}}<ref>{{cite web
 | title = A019692 – OEIS
 | work= [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]]
 | publisher= OEIS Foundation Inc.
 | url = https://oeis.org/A019692
 | access-date = 2026-03-19
}}</ref>

They constitute the sequence A019692 in the [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|OEIS]].

== History ==

The use of {{math|''τ''}} or of other dedicated symbols for {{math|2''π''}} in lieu of {{math|''π''}} has been advocated by several mathematicians and other proponents in recent decades. The number 6.28... has been historically studied and denoted by various symbols, but in the 18th century, {{math|''π''}} became the universally-understood symbol for 3.14... instead.

=== {{math|''τ''}} notation proposal ===
The proposal to use the Greek letter {{math|''τ''}} as a circle constant representing {{math|2''π''}} dates to [[Michael Hartl]]'s 2010 publication, ''The Tau Manifesto'',{{efn|name="Hartl-refs"|Original version,<ref name="Hartl_2010" /> current version<ref name="Hartl_2019" />}} although the symbol had been independently suggested earlier by Joseph Lindenburg ({{circa|1990}}), John Fisher (2004) and Peter Harremoës (2010).<ref>{{cite AV media |people=sudgylacmoe; Hartl, Michael |date=28 June 2023 |title=The Tau Manifesto – With Michael Hartl |type=YouTube video |language=English |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kMtgV18Iew8 |access-date=24 July 2024 |time=18:35 |time-caption= Information shown at}}</ref>

Hartl offered two reasons for the choice of notation. First, {{math|''τ''}} is the number of radians in one ''turn'', and both {{math|''τ''}} and ''turn'' begin with a {{IPAc-en|t}} sound. Second, {{math|''τ''}} visually resembles {{math|''π''}}, whose association with the circle constant is unavoidable. Moreover, Hartl asserted that the use of a familiar Greek letter like {{math|''τ''}} was preferable to the choice of a completely new symbol (like Bob Palais' proposed symbol {{tmath|1= \pi\!\;\!\!\!\pi}}), since people would be immediately able to pronounce it when they encounter it.

=== Earlier proposals ===
There had been a number of earlier proposals for a new circle constant equal to {{math|2''π''}}, together with varying suggestions for its name and symbol.

In 2001, Dr. Bob Palais of the [[University of Utah]] asserted that {{math|''π''}} is "wrong" as the fundamental circle constant and that {{math|2''π''}} was the proper value.<ref name="Palais_2001" /> He proposed using a "{{math|''π''}} with three legs" symbol to denote the constant ({{tmath|1= \pi\!\;\!\!\!\pi = 2\pi }}), and referred to angles as fractions of a "turn" ({{tmath|1= \tfrac 1 4 \pi\!\;\!\!\!\pi = \tfrac 1 4\,\mathrm{turn} }}). Palais stated that the word "turn" served as both the name of the new constant and a reference to the ordinary language meaning of [[Turn (angle)|turn]].<ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=Pi Is Wrong! |url=https://www.math.utah.edu/~palais/pi.html |access-date=2025-04-26 |website=www.math.utah.edu}}</ref>

In 2008, [[Robert P. Crease]] proposed defining a constant as the ratio of circumference to radius, an idea supported by [[John Horton Conway]], who is cited to have said that "{{math|2''π''}} is obviously the correct constant".<ref name=":2">{{cite magazine |last=Crease |first=Robert |date=2008-02-01 |title=Constant failure |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/constant-failure/ |magazine=Physics World |publisher=Institute of Physics |access-date=2024-08-03}}</ref>

The same year, Thomas Colignatus proposed the uppercase Greek letter [[theta]], {{math|Θ}}, to represent {{math|2''π''}} due to its visual resemblance of a circle.<ref name="Cool_2008" /> For a similar reason another proposal suggested the Phoenician and Hebrew letter [[teth]], 𐤈 or ט, (from which the letter theta was derived), due to its connection with wheels and circles in ancient cultures.<ref name="Mann-Janzen-Ali-Scourboutakos-Guleria_2015" /><ref name="Mann-Chen-Aylward-Jorritsma-Mann-Defaz-Pierce-Lam-Stairs-Hermandez-Li-Xiang-Kanaan_2019" />

=== Historical use of other symbols to represent 6.28... ===
{{see also|Pi#Adoption of the symbol π}}

The number 6.28... has been studied historically long before contemporary proposals to name it {{math|''τ''}}. In 1424, [[Jamshid al-Kashi]] computed the number 6.28... to 9 [[sexagesimal]] ([[radix|base]] 60) digits.<ref>''Al-Kashi'', author: Adolf P. Youschkevitch, chief editor: Boris A. Rosenfeld, p. 256</ref> The first 16 sexagesimal digits of {{math|''τ''}} are: {{gaps|6;16,59,28,|1,34,51,|46,14,49,|55,12,35,|26,8,58,..}}<ref>{{cite web | title = A091649 – OEIS | work = [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]] | publisher = OEIS Foundation Inc. | url = https://oeis.org/A091649 | access-date = 2026-03-19 }}</ref>

The meaning of the symbol {{math|''π''}} was not originally defined as the ratio of circumference to diameter, and at times was used in representations of the constant 6.28...&nbsp;.

Early works in circle geometry used the letter {{math|''π''}} to designate the [[perimeter]] (i.e., [[circumference]]) in different fractional representations of circle constants and in 1697 [[David Gregory (mathematician)|David Gregory]] used {{math|{{sfrac|''π''|''ρ''}}}} (pi over rho) to denote the perimeter divided by the radius (6.28...).<ref name="Beckmann_1989" /><ref name="Schwartzman_1994" />

Subsequently {{math|''π''}} came to be used as a single symbol to represent the ratios in whole. [[Leonhard Euler]] initially used the single letter {{math|''π''}} to denote the constant 6.28... in his 1727 ''Essay Explaining the Properties of Air''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Euler |first=Leonhard |date=1727 |title=Tentamen explicationis phaenomenorum aeris|url=http://eulerarchive.maa.org/docs/originals/E007.pdf#page=5 |journal=Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitana 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160401072718/http://eulerarchive.maa.org/docs/originals/E007.pdf#page=5|archive-date=1 April 2016|url-status=live}} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610172054/http://www.17centurymaths.com/contents/euler/e007tr.pdf#page=3 |date=10 June 2016 }}: "{{mvar|π}} is taken for the ratio of the radius to the periphery [note that in this work, Euler's {{math|''π''}} is double our {{math|''π''}}.]"</ref><ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3C1iHFBXVEcC&pg=PA139 |title=Lettres inédites Elsewhere in ''Mechanica'', Euler instead used the letter {{math|''π''}} for one-fourth of the circumference of a unit circle, or 1.57... .<ref>{{cite book |last=Euler |first=Leonhard |date=1736 |title=Mechanica sive motus scientia analytice exposita |url=https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/euler-works/15/ |page=185 |access-date=2025-02-12}}</ref><ref name="Sanderson-2018">{{cite AV media |people=Sanderson, Grant |date=2018-03-14 |title=How pi was almost 6.283185... |language=English |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bcPTiiiYDs8 |access-date=2025-02-11 |time=2:29}}</ref> Usage of the letter {{math|''π''}}, sometimes for 3.14... and other times for 6.28..., became widespread, with the convention varying as late as 1761;<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P-hEAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA374 |title=Cursus Mathematicus: Elementorum Analyseos Infinitorum Elementorum Analyseos Infinitorvm |last=Segner |first=Johann Andreas von |date=1761 |publisher=Renger |page=374 |language=la |quote=Si autem {{math|''π''}} notet peripheriam circuli, cuius diameter eſt {{math|2}}}}</ref> afterward, the use of {{math|''π''}} for 3.14... exclusively became standard, as a result of the influence of Euler's later works.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |date=2024-03-14 |title=Pi |url=https://www.britannica.com/science/pi-mathematics |access-date=2024-03-26 |website=Encyclopaedia Britannica |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Euler_1746" />

== Notation using ''τ'' ==

Proponents argue that while use of {{math|''τ''}} in place of {{math|2''π''}} does not change any of the underlying mathematics, it does lead to simpler and more intuitive notation in many areas. Michael Hartl's ''Tau Manifesto''{{efn|name="Hartl-refs"}} gives many examples of formulas that are asserted to be clearer where {{math|''τ''}} is used instead of {{math|''π''}}.<ref name="Aron_2011" /><ref name="Landau_2011" /><ref name="Bartholomew_2014" />

=== Units of angle ===
Hartl and Robert Palais<ref name=":1" /> have argued that {{math|''τ''}} allows angles to be expressed more directly and in a way that makes clear the link between the radian measure and rotation around the unit circle.

Since an angle (in radians) of <math>\tau</math> corresponds to a [[turn (angle)|turn]], an angle (in radians) given as a fraction of <math>\tau</math> corresponds to the same fraction of a turn. (This is not the case if the angle is expressed as a fraction of <math>\pi</math> instead, in which case it would correspond to the same fraction of a half-turn, not of a whole turn.) For instance, {{math|{{sfrac|3|4}}''τ'' rad}} can be easily interpreted as {{math|{{sfrac|3|4}}}} of a turn, in contrast with the same angle written as {{math|{{sfrac|3|2}}''π'' rad}}, where the meaning could be less intuitive. For this reason, Hartl has argued that the use of {{math|''π''}} in mathematical education is pedagogically detrimental, and that using {{math|''τ''}} would improve clarity in mathematical teaching regarding [[trigonometry]] and [[radian]]s.

Critics have responded that a full rotation is not necessarily the correct or fundamental reference measure for angles and two other possibilities, the [[right angle]] and straight angle, each have historical precedent. [[Euclidean geometry#System of measurement and arithmetic|Euclid]] used the right angle as the basic unit of angle, and David Butler has suggested that {{math|1={{sfrac|1|4}}''τ'' = {{sfrac|1|2}}''π'' ≈ 1.57}}, which he denotes with the Greek letter {{math|''η''}} ([[eta]]), should be seen as the fundamental circle constant.<ref>{{cite web |last=Butler |first=David |title=Pi, Tau and Eta |url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/mathslearning/news/list/2011/06/08/pi-tau-and-eta |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250417064300/https://www.adelaide.edu.au/mathslearning/news/list/2011/06/08/pi-tau-and-eta|archive-date=2025-04-17}}</ref>

=== Trigonometric functions ===
[[File:Standard Trigonometric Functions.svg|thumb|Plots of common trigonometric functions (sin, cos, tan, cot, sec, csc) with ''x''-axis running from −τ through +τ]]
Hartl has argued that the periodic [[trigonometric functions]] are simplified when using {{math|τ}}, as it corresponds to the [[periodic function|period]] of the [[sine and cosine]] functions: {{math|sin}} repeats with [[periodic function|period]] {{math|1=''T'' = ''τ''}}, reaches a maximum at {{math|1={{sfrac|1|4}}''T'' = {{sfrac|1|4}}''τ''}} and a minimum at {{math|1={{sfrac|3|4}}''T'' = {{sfrac|3|4}}''τ''}}. (By contrast, {{math|''π''}} is only half the period of the <math>\sin</math> and <math>\cos</math> functions.)

More generally, given constants <math>\omega</math> and <math>\phi</math>, a [[sine wave|sinusoidal]] function of the form <math>t \mapsto \cos(\omega t + \phi)</math> or <math>t \mapsto \sin(\omega t + \phi)</math> has the [[periodic function|period]] <math>T=\frac{\tau}{\omega}</math>, and the number of periods in each interval of length 1 is <math>f=\frac{1}{T}=\frac{\omega}{\tau}</math>. Here, <math>\omega</math> can be interpreted as an [[angular frequency]] and <math>f</math> as a [[rotational frequency]].

As a result, in contexts related to sinusoidal waves or periodic rotation, <math>\tau=2\pi</math> is the conversion factor between quantities corresponding to numbers of [[turn (angle)|turns]] or periods (i.e. [[rotational frequency|frequencies]]) and quantities corresponding to numbers of [[radian]]s or [[phase (waves)|phase]] units (i.e. [[angular frequency|angular frequencies]]). For instance:

* [[angular frequency]] <math>\omega</math> is equal to {{math|''τ''}} times the [[rotational frequency]] <math>f</math> (or, equivalently, to {{math|''τ''}} divided by the [[frequency|period duration]] <math>T</math>);
* angular [[wavenumber]] <math>k</math> is equal to {{math|''τ''}} times the ordinary [[wavenumber]] <math>\tilde{\nu}</math> (or, equivalently, to {{math|''τ''}} divided by the [[wavelength|spatial period]] <math>\lambda</math>).


The following table shows particular values of the [[sine and cosine|sin]], [[sine and cosine|cos]] and [[trigonometric functions|tan]] functions, for arguments expressed in terms of {{math|''τ''}}:

<math>
\begin{alignat}{3}
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{16}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt{2}}}{2} &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{16}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}}{2} &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{16}\right) &= \sqrt{2}-1 \\[0.6em]
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{12}\right) &= \frac{1}{2} &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{12}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{12}\right) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\[0.6em]
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{10}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{10-2\sqrt{5}}}{4} &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{10}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{4} &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{10}\right) &= \sqrt{5-2\sqrt{5}} \\[0.6em]
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{8}\right) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{8}\right) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{8}\right) &= 1 \\[0.6em]
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{6}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{6}\right) &= \frac{1}{2} &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{6}\right) &= \sqrt{3} \\[0.6em]
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{5}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{10+2\sqrt{5}}}{4} &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{5}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4} &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{5}\right) &= \sqrt{5+2\sqrt{5}} \\[0.6em]
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{4}\right) &= 1 &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{4}\right) &= 0 &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{4}\right) &\text{ is undefined (or ∞)} \\[0.6em]
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{3}\right) &= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{3}\right) &= \frac{-1}{2} &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{3}\right) &= -\sqrt{3} \\[0.6em]
\sin\left(\frac{\tau}{2}\right) &= 0 &\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{\tau}{2}\right) &= -1 &\qquad
\tan\left(\frac{\tau}{2}\right) &= 0 \\[0.6em]
\sin(\tau) &= 0 &\qquad
\cos(\tau) &= 1 &\qquad
\tan(\tau) &= 0
\end{alignat}
</math>

=== Area of a circle ===
Critics have argued that the formula for the [[area of a circle]] {{math|1=''A'' = ''πr''<sup>2</sup>}} is more complicated when restated as {{math|1=''A'' = {{sfrac|1|2}}''τr''<sup>2</sup>}}. Hartl and others have responded that the {{sfrac|1|2}} factor is meaningful, arising from either [[Integral|integration]] or geometric proofs for the area of a circle as [[Area of a circle#Triangle proof|half the circumference times the radius]]. Moreover, Hartl has argued that {{math|{{sfrac|1|2}}''τr''<sup>2</sup>}} can be seen as a special case of the more general formula {{math|{{sfrac|1|2}}''θr''<sup>2</sup>}} for the area of a [[circular arc#Sector area|circular sector]] spanned by the angle {{math|''θ''}} when {{math|''θ''}} is taken to be {{math|τ}} (a whole turn).

=== Euler's identity and roots of unity ===
[[Euler's identity]], {{math|1=''e''<sup>''iπ''</sup> + 1 = 0}}, sometimes claimed to be "the most beautiful theorem in mathematics"<ref>{{cite web |last=Peshin |first=Akash |date=2017-12-24 |title=Euler's Identity: 'The Most Beautiful Theorem In Mathematics' |url=https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/eulers-identity-beautiful-theorem-mathematics.html |access-date=2025-04-27 |website=ScienceABC |language=en-US}}</ref>, becomes {{math|1=''e''<sup>i''τ''/2 </sup> + 1 = 0}} in terms of <math>\tau</math>. Hartl has asserted that {{math|1=''e''<sup>''iτ''</sup> = 1}} (which he also called "Euler's identity") is a more fundamental and meaningful equation.

John Conway noted<ref name=":2" /> that Euler's identity is a specific case of the general formula of the {{math|''n''}}th [[roots of unity]], {{math|1={{radic|1|''n''}} = ''e''<sup>''iτk/n''</sup> (''k'' = 1, 2, ..., ''n'')}}, which he maintained is preferable and more economical than Euler's identity.

=== Higher-dimensional spheres and balls ===

While {{math|''τ''}} corresponds to the circumference of a unit circle in a two-dimensional Euclidean plane, the situation is more complicated in higher dimensions, where the formulas for the [[n-sphere#Volume and surface area|volume and surface area of a hypersphere in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces]] involve fractions and powers of {{math|''π''}} (or {{math|''τ''}}).

For a given integer {{mvar|n}}, the following formulas yield the generalized volume <math>V_n</math> and surface area <math>S_{n-1}</math> of a {{mvar|n}}-dimensional unit hypersphere (in {{mvar|n}}-dimensional Euclidean space):

<math display="block">{\displaystyle
S_{n-1} = \frac{2 \pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n}{2}\bigr)} = \frac{(\frac{\pi}{2})^{\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor} \cdot 2^n}{(n-2)!!}; \quad
V_n     = \frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n}{2} + 1\bigr)} = \frac{(\frac{\pi}{2})^{\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor} \cdot 2^n}{n!!}
}
</math>

or equivalently in terms of {{math|''τ''}} instead of {{math|''π''}}:

<math display="block">
S_{n-1} = \frac{2 (\frac{\tau}{2})^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n}{2}\bigr)} = \frac{(\frac{\tau}{4})^{\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor} \cdot 2^n}{(n-2)!!}; \quad
V_n     = \frac{(\frac{\tau}{2})^{n/2}}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n}{2} + 1\bigr)} = \frac{(\frac{\tau}{4})^{\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor} \cdot 2^n}{n!!}
</math>

where <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[gamma function|Euler gamma function]] and <math>!!</math> denotes the [[double factorial]].

Moreover, there exist the following recurrence relations between successive values of <math>V_n</math> and <math>S_n</math>:

<math>V_n = \frac{S_{n-1}}{n}; \quad S_n = \tau V_{n-1}</math>

For the first values of the dimension {{mvar|n}}, the values of the generalized volume <math>V_n</math> and surface area <math>S_{n-1}</math> of a unit hypersphere are as follows, here expressed in terms of {{math|''τ''}} instead of {{math|''π''}}:

|-
| 1
| <math>2</math>
| <math>2</math>
|-
| 2

| <math>\tau</math>

Only when the dimension {{math|''n''}} is 2 does {{math|''τ''}} have a privileged status as the circumference of the unit circle (the unit circle being a 2-dimensional ball, and circumference corresponding to generalized 1-dimensional volume). In higher dimensions, the particular choice of the constant {{math|''τ''}} instead of {{math|''π''}} becomes less advantageous. However, Hartl argues that circles and angles in the two-dimensional case are far more frequently encountered than higher-dimensional cases, and that it thus makes sense for the choice of the named constant {{math|''τ''}} to correspond to circumference in the two-dimensional case.

== In programming languages and calculators ==

The following table documents various programming languages that have implemented the circle constant for converting between turns and radians. All of the languages below support the name "Tau" in some casing, but Processing also supports "TWO_PI" and Raku also supports the symbol "τ" for accessing the same value.

The constant {{math|''τ''}} is made available in the Google calculator, [[Desmos|Desmos graphing calculator]],<ref name="Desmos" />  and the [[iPhone]]'s Convert Angle option expresses the turn as {{math|''τ''}}.<ref name="Gadget Hacks" />
